readerTitle: Why a marketplace's best matches can walk out the door
caseNote: 가상 사례 (도매 마켓플레이스, 반려견 산책 앱) + 실제 관찰 (반복 거래가 많은 마켓플레이스에서 플랫폼 밖 거래가 흔하다는 일반적 패턴) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 좋은 연결이 반복될수록 플랫폼을 떠날 이유도 커진다. 그래서 마켓플레이스는 만남이 아니라 매번의 거래에서 가치를 줘야 한다.
misconception: 좋은 매칭을 많이 만들수록 마켓플레이스 매출은 자연스럽게 늘어난다. 이탈은 연락처 공유를 막으면 해결된다.

sources.text: 마켓플레이스 운영에서 널리 쓰이는 개념 (disintermediation, platform leakage)
모든 수치와 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 도매 사례 계산: 플랫폼 경유 시 가게 $1,000 지불, 수수료 15% $150, 생산자 수령 $850. 직거래 10% 할인 시 가게 $900 지불(−$100 절약), 생산자 $900 수령(+$50). 연 12회 주문이면 플랫폼 손실 $150 × 12 = $1,800.
softwareNote의 프리랜서 플랫폼 '우회 금지 조항'은 업계의 일반적 관행으로만 서술했습니다. 특정 회사명이나 기간·수수료는 넣지 않았습니다. 게시 전 표현이 과장되지 않았는지 확인하세요.
반복적·관계 중심 거래(청소, 과외, 산책 등)에서 플랫폼 이탈이 잦다는 내용은 일반적 관찰로 서술했습니다. 특정 기업의 실패 원인으로 단정하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The marketplace's best matches were its worst customers.
body: A wholesale website connects independent shops with small food producers. A gift shop finds a local jam maker and orders through the site. The jam sells fast.
The second box arrives with a handwritten card: "Order direct next time. Save 10%." The shop never orders through the site again.

image.label: Jam box with a handwritten card tucked inside
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 가게 계산대 위에 잼 병이 든 배송 상자, 상자 안에 손글씨 카드 "Order direct, save 10%". 배경에 흐릿한 노트북 화면(웹사이트, 로고 없음). 실제 브랜드나 로고 사용 금지.

cards.title: Repeat orders keep vanishing.
body: You run that wholesale site and take 15% of each order. Your data shows a pattern: once a shop and a producer have traded twice, their orders on your site drop sharply.

options.text: Hide phone numbers and emails, and ban sellers who share them
options.feedback: It may slow leaks, but buyers and sellers need to talk. You annoy your best users, and the jam card still fits in the box.

options.text: Add things that make every order easier: 60-day payment terms, returns, one invoice for all suppliers
options.feedback: It costs you money and effort to provide, but now staying on the site saves both sides something each time they order, not just the first time.

options.text: Cut your fee from 15% to 8% on repeat orders
options.feedback: It shrinks the reward for leaving, but a phone call is still free. You give up margin without giving a new reason to stay.

cards.title: Going direct makes both sides richer.
body: The shop saves $100. The jam maker earns $50 more. The only loser is the site, which loses $150 an order, or **$1,800 a year** if the pair orders monthly.

breakdown.label: On the site
breakdown.detail: Shop pays; site keeps 15%, maker gets $850

breakdown.label: Direct
breakdown.detail: Shop pays 10% less; maker keeps all of it

cards.title: Disintermediation
body: An *intermediary* is a middleman. **Disintermediation** is when the two sides use a marketplace to find each other, then cut it out and deal directly.
Here's the twist. The better the match, the more likely it leaves. A happy shop and a reliable maker have every reason to keep trading, and no reason to keep paying someone to introduce them.

image.label: A bridge between two shops, with people walking around it
image.brief: 단순한 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 가게, 오른쪽 생산자, 가운데 다리(마켓플레이스). 첫 거래는 다리 위로, 이후 거래는 다리 옆 지름길 점선으로 오가는 모습. 다리 위에 "15%" 표지판.

cards.title: Some marketplaces leak more than others.
body: Leaks are most likely when a few conditions stack up:
list: **Repeat deals** between the same two parties
**Large orders**, so the fee is worth avoiding
**A personal relationship**, so trust no longer needs the platform
**Easy to do alone**, once you have a phone number
cards.callout: One-off purchases, like a hotel in a city you visit once, leak far less.

cards.title: Marketplaces that keep deals earn their fee every time.
body: Some charge for what they truly provide: a fee for the introduction, then little or nothing after. Others do real work on each deal, like payment protection, delivery, insurance or record-keeping.
The question to ask is simple: what would both sides lose if they went direct tomorrow?
cards.softwareNote: Freelance platforms often ban moving clients off-site in their terms. What keeps work on the platform in practice tends to be the tools: contracts, held payments, time tracking and invoices that both sides would otherwise rebuild by hand.

cards.title: Fighting leaks can cost more than the leaks.
body: Blocking contact details frustrates honest users and can push your best sellers to leave entirely. Raising fees to make up lost revenue gives everyone a bigger reason to go direct.
And some leakage is fine. If your real value is the first match, charge clearly for that and accept that strong pairs will graduate.

cards.title: Now it's a dog-walking app.
body: Your app matches dog owners with local walkers and takes 20% per walk. Most owners book the same walker three times a week. After a month, many stop booking through the app.
Which change best fits the problem?

options.text: Keep 20%, hide walker surnames, and warn owners not to pay in cash
options.feedback: Easy to set up, but owners hand over house keys to these walkers. They'll swap numbers anyway and resent the app.

options.text: Charge owners a monthly plan that includes insurance, live walk tracking and a backup walker on sick days
options.feedback: Each feature costs you something to run, but owners lose real protection by going direct, so the app is worth paying for every week.

options.text: Charge a one-time matching fee and let pairs go free afterward
options.feedback: Honest pricing for an introduction, but you give up the ongoing revenue from your most loyal pairs.

cards.title: A marketplace must be worth it on the tenth deal, not just the first.
body: If your only value is the introduction, your best matches will leave. Price the introduction, or add value to every deal.
**Try it today:** list what your customers would lose if they dealt directly with each other tomorrow. If the list is short, that's your leak.
